papers.title: MaaD-TAD: an all-atom model of the duplicated PRAMEF/HNRNPCL chromatin domain built from sequence homology
papers.abstract: In the nucleus, the placement of genes in the 3D fold of DNA affects how they function. Models of this fold use two kinds of data: contact maps constructed from Hi-C, and nucleosome maps showing where DNA is wound around nucleosomes. Over evolution, sections of the genome were copied, creating near-identical regions. Reads from these regions cannot be assigned to one copy and are discarded, leaving "void regions" in both maps. We tested MaaD-TAD, a pipeline that models topologically associating domains (TADs) at the atomic level, on the PRAMEF/HNRNPCL locus on human chromosome 1. This challenging locus spans 652 kb, with only 15% of its nucleosome positions known and most contact data missing. To test our hypothesis that copies with similar sequence lie close in space, i.e. homology as a surrogate for proximity, we constructed a map of sequence homology in place of Hi-C and used CSynth to fold it into a 3D path. We then lengthened the path to fit a chromatin fibre, and refined the model by adding cohesin complexes, which stabilize chromatin structure. Cohesin is a ring-shaped protein complex through which a loop of chromatin is threaded; the loop is commonly anchored by CTCF proteins bound on either leg. Using known databases, we placed CTCF sites in our model and joined three to their copies with cohesin rings; in each pair the sites face each other, as loop anchors do. The final model holds 3,359 nucleosomes and about 55 million atoms. Micro-C, an advanced, higher-resolution form of Hi-C, provided data on two other duplicated regions that support our hypothesis: matching copies touched 1.2 to 1.9 times more often than expected. Our approach provides a novel method to reconstruct DNA regions with absent contact data and, to our knowledge, the first all-atom model of a complete TAD.

papers.title: Genomes of Solenogastres Shed Light on Ancestral Molluscan Biomineralization Genes
papers.abstract: Aplacophora (Solenogastres + Caudofoveata) is a group of worm-like molluscs that lack a shell and instead are covered with aragonitic spines and scales called sclerites. Sclerites are also found along the girdle in chitons (Polyplacophora) and are a synapomorphy for Aculifera (Aplacophora + Polyplacophora), which is the sister taxon of all other shell-bearing molluscs (Conchifera). However, whether the same genetic mechanism underlies the process of biomineralization in aculiferans and conchiferans is unknown. To investigate evolution of genes involved in biomineralization across Mollusca, we re-sequenced the genomes of two species of Solenogastres, Epimenia babai and Neomenia megatrapezata , producing near-chromosome-level assemblies through PacBio HiFi and Hi-C scaffolding. Using a combination of orthology inference and similarity searches against a known SMP database we identified 1,244 putative SMP orthogroups across Mollusca, 292 of which were present in at least one solenogaster genome. SMPs undergoing significant expansion/contraction at key nodes were further investigated. Of these, 15 were found in at least one solenogaster genome and included families containing chitin-binding, von Willebrand factor A, and C-type lectin domains. Across Mollusca, Solenogastres showed the highest number of significant losses in all gene families, including the SMPs investigated. Targeted searches for structural, silk-like proteins in Aculifera show further reductions in Solenogastres (16-17) compared to caudofoveates (29) and chitons (46-80). Altogether, our results support a conserved but reduced biomineralization toolkit underlying sclerite formation in Solenogastres and identify candidate genes for further proteomic and functional study.

papers.title: Systematic promoter perturbation reveals limitations of AlphaGenome gene expression predictions
papers.abstract: Sequence-to-function (S2F) models promise to facilitate the interpretation of noncoding variants by predicting their effects on gene regulation directly from genomic sequence. However, whether these models recapitulate fundamental principles of transcriptional biology remains unclear. Here, we tested whether AlphaGenome recognizes the expected consequences of promoter disruption on predicted gene expression. We systematically perturbed annotated promoter elements in silico for 2,111 promoter-gene pairs using dinucleotide shuffling, GC-adjusted random base substitution, and N-masking. We then compared AlphaGenome-predicted CAGE and RNA-sequencing signals across 20 tissues for reference and promoter-disrupted sequences. While CAGE and RNA-sequencing predictions were strongly correlated for reference sequences, promoter disruption markedly reduced predicted CAGE activity, with N masking producing reductions of approximately three orders of magnitude. By contrast, the predicted RNA-sequencing signals were substantially less affected, resulting in an uncoupling of two molecular readouts of gene expression. Exon-level analyses showed that AlphaGenome predicted reduced RNA-sequencing signal when exonic sequences are within the disrupted region, but frequently failed to propagate this effect to downstream exons. This divergence between the CAGE and RNA-sequencing readouts was apparent from the second exon onward and was more pronounced in longer genes. Although alternative transcription initiation and shared downstream exons may explain individual cases, it is unlikely to account for the systematic discordance between CAGE and RNA-sequencing predictions. These findings indicate that AlphaGenome can recognize the local loss of promoter activity without consistently capturing its consequences across the corresponding transcript. More broadly, our results show that predictions from individual S2F output tracks do not necessarily reflect a coherent model of transcription. Systematic biological benchmarking and experimental validation therefore remain essential before such predictions can be used to prioritize or classify noncoding variants in research or diagnostic settings.

papers.title: Integrative Transcriptomic Analysis Reveals Differential Exon Usage and Virulence Gene Family Dynamics in Plasmodium falciparum during Severe Malaria
papers.abstract: Malaria remains a leading cause of child mortality in developing countries, with roughly 610,000 deaths per year. While the disease is caused by five human Plasmodium species, Plasmodium falciparum (Pf ) causes the most severe form. Progression from uncomplicated to severe malaria is characterized by high proliferation of the parasite, severely affecting children under five years old. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying disease progression remain an active area of research. Many multicopy genes have been implicated in Pf virulence. Some of these genes are implicated in cytoadherence, host-cell invasion, immune evasion, sequestration of infected erythrocytes, and antigenic variation. We employed an integrative transcriptomic analysis in this study to elucidate the molecular underpinnings of severe malaria and gene expression patterns, virulence gene dynamics, and the potential contribution of alternative splicing. Results show an overexpression of protein synthesis and ribosomal genes associated with severe malaria. About 86% (n=1865) of all differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were downregulated in severe malaria, and 226 genes exhibited both differential expression and differential exon usage (DEU). Pf virulence genes and antigenic genes such as var (pfEMP1), stevor, surfin, rif (rifin), ptm-2TM, and msp were upregulated in severe malaria compared with uncomplicated malaria, except for rifin. In severe malaria, there was evidence of co-expression and regulation within multigene families, as well as DEU and alternative splicing in virulence genes and antimalarial resistance-related proteins. Pf does not employ a single mechanism for disease progression but suppresses and deregulates nonessential pathways, processes, and genes, which are upregulated virulence genes, DNA replication, mRNA transcription, and protein synthesis. Multicopy genes are co-expressed and regulated to meet the molecular needs of the parasite. The parasite employs alternative splicing and DEU mechanisms for immune invasion and evasion, host-parasite interaction, as well as antimalarial resistance.

papers.title: Population Genomics of the Bovine Sialic Acid Network Reveals Functional and Evolutionary Diversity Across European and South African Cattle Breeds
papers.abstract: **Background:** Sialic acids, mainly N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac) and N-glycolylneuraminic acid (Neu5Gc), are terminal monosaccharides of glycans involved in numerous physiological processes, such as immune and neuronal function. Their biosynthesis, transport, transfer and turnover depend on a network of genes, but genetic studies in cattle have mostly addressed individual genes or genetic associations with milk oligosaccharide concentrations, leaving variation across this network largely uncharacterized. In bovine milk, sialylated glycans that depend on this network vary among animals and change rapidly during early lactation. We therefore characterized variation in 13 selected genes of the bovine sialic acid network using whole-genome sequence data from European and South African cattle. **Results:** We analyzed 346 animals from 12 European and 4 South African breeds. Of 9,724 variants in the 13 target genes, 8,675 were intronic and 62 were predicted to alter the amino acid sequence. Integration of SIFT predictions, Rate4Site conservation and protein context, with population representation as supporting evidence, identified 15 prioritized candidates, including 7 high-priority candidates in NEU3, ST8SIA2, ST8SIA4, CMAH and ST3GAL4. The most differentiated candidates were not among the 15 prioritized variants. NEU3 Y136H showed the largest regional contrast in allele frequency (0.83 in South African and 0.34 in European cattle), whereas several prioritized candidates were represented by a single allele in the South African cohort. Genome-wide principal component analysis of 950,219 linkage-disequilibrium-pruned SNPs separated South African from European cattle along the first component, which explained about 25% of the variance. None of the 220 analyzed common pathway SNPs exceeded the corresponding genome-wide differentiation thresholds at breed, country or regional level. Within the ascertained pathway SNPs, diversity was higher in South African breeds, and Tajima's D was shifted toward positive values in European breeds and centered near zero in South African breeds. **Conclusions:** This study provides a network-wide map of predicted protein-altering variation in the bovine sialic acid pathway and identifies 15 candidates for functional investigation, most of them rare. Because the most differentiated variants were not those with the strongest functional support, population contrasts, evolutionary conservation and protein context provide complementary evidence for selecting candidates. The analyzed common pathway SNPs did not show exceptional differentiation relative to the genome-wide background. The candidates provide specific targets for genotyping, enzyme-level testing and genotype-informed milk phenotyping.

papers.title: Integrating bacterial genomics and host transcriptomics links Burkholderia pseudomallei variation to melioidosis mortality and neutrophil responses
papers.abstract: Bacterial genetic variation contributes to the outcome of infection, but its relationship with host immune responses is rarely investigated in the same patients, limiting the biological interpretation of pathogen-associated disease severity. Here, we integrated pathogen genomics, clinical outcomes and host transcriptomics to investigate host-pathogen interactions in melioidosis, a frequently fatal infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. We analysed prospective clinical data from 2,142 patients, whole-genome sequences from 2,101 infecting isolates and 646 paired host blood transcriptomes across five cohorts collected between 2012 and 2023. Infections were typically dominated by a single strain, with limited within-host diversification, supporting the use of an infecting isolate genome to investigate pathogen-associated clinical outcomes. Bacterial genome-wide association studies identified one locus associated with binary mortality at genome-wide significance. Incorporating patient age, sex, body mass index and Charlson Comorbidity Index increased this to four, while modelling time to death as a continuous phenotype identified seven loci. Integration with paired host transcriptomes linked mortality-associated bacterial genetic variation to imputed signatures of increased immature neutrophils and reduced neutrophil degranulation. An intergenic region upstream of the polyketide synthesis locus BPSS1006-BPSS1011 was additionally associated with downregulation of host genes involved in myeloid-cell signalling and cell proliferation pathways. These findings connect naturally occurring B. pseudomallei genomic variation associated with mortality to distinct host immune signatures, providing insight into pathogen-host interactions underlying severe melioidosis and a framework for investigating the contribution of pathogen genetic diversity to clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Personalised Gene Expression Prediction Improves Cell-Type-Specific Association Testing
papers.abstract: Linking genetic variation to disease requires accurate prediction of its effects on gene expression in relevant cell types. Sequence-to-function models offer a way to predict these effects and, with training on personal genomes, have begun to capture inter-individual expression differences. However, effect sign accuracy remains limited, and predictive uncertainty is unquantified. Here we introduce ATTICUS, which combines personalised sequence representations with uncertainty-aware expression prediction. ATTICUS transfers regulatory information learned in bulk expression pretraining to cell-type-specific expression prediction without requiring genotypes paired with single-cell expression data. Across blood and brain cell types in OneK1K and ROSMAP, ATTICUS approximately doubles expression prediction correlations relative to scPrediXcan and substantially improves sign accuracy. Moreover, ATTICUS enables uncertainty-aware transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS). Applied to systemic lupus erythematosus and Alzheimer's disease, ATTICUS identifies more associations, with greater cell-type specificity and stronger directional concordance, and reduced statistical inflation. Together, our results demonstrate that personalised training makes predictions more directionally consistent, and uncertainty propagation improves the calibration of TWAS and the prioritisation of disease genes. ATTICUS provides a framework for both, enabling the use of single-cell expression datasets without matched genotypes to inform uncertainty-aware TWAS, expanding their use in prioritising disease-associated genes and cell types.

papers.title: Transcriptome profiling reveals gene regulatory network governing seed size in Brassica napus
papers.abstract: Seed size is a critical trait influencing yield and quality in oilseed crops such as Brassica napus. Despite their economic importance, the genetic and molecular mechanisms regulating seed size remain unclear, particularly in polyploid species, such as B. napus. To deepen our understanding of seed size regulation, we performed a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis across four developmental stages (heart, torpedo, green, and mature) and three distinct seed organs: the seed coat, embryo, and endosperm. Differential expression analysis between B. napus var. Zhongshuang (ZS11) and B. napus cv. Ragged Jack (RJ) was performed to uncover regulatory networks involved in seed size control. Our results uncovered dynamic gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and pinpointed key regulators, including well-established factors like ABI5 and BRI1, as well as novel candidate genes such as KNAT5, ARF11, SUS2, UGT72B1, UGT89A2, and SBT1.7. The present research provides an understanding of the regulatory networks governing seed size in B. napus. These findings not only enhance our knowledge of seed biology but also offer valuable resources for future breeding strategies aimed at optimizing seed size and yield in polyploid oilseed crops.

papers.title: Segment-dependent phylogenetic resolution reveals geographic and host sampling gaps in Oropouche virus genomes
papers.abstract: Background. Oropouche virus (OROV) has been reported in areas beyond its historical Amazonian range since 2023, accompanied by rapid growth in publicly available genomic data. However, the extent to which these data provide reliable phylogenetic and epidemiological resolution, and whether that resolution differs among genome segments, has not been systematically examined. Methods. Nucleotide sequences annotated under Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense were retrieved from NCBI Virus (accessed 13 May 2025) and filtered to retain records at least 70% of the reference length for each segment, yielding 898 S, 831 M, and 832 L sequences. Segments were aligned independently with MAFFT, and maximum-likelihood phylogenies were inferred with IQ-TREE using ModelFinder and ultrafast bootstrap approximation. Trees were annotated with collection date, country, and host in iTOL. Results. Phylogenetic resolution differed among segments. Contemporary Brazilian sequences formed a largely unresolved region in the S segment tree, whereas the M and L trees resolved recent clusters to differing degrees. Resolution did not track segment length: the M tree resolved contemporary structure more strongly than the longer L tree, and total tree length was approximately 3.5 times greater in the M tree despite near-identical taxon sampling. Sequences collected before 2010 were recovered in supported clusters in all three segment trees, although their configuration differed by segment. These sequences were also predominantly non-Brazilian and non-human, preventing collection date, geographic origin, and host from being separated as explanations for the observed clustering. The species-level query also retained three reassortant viruses, which may influence segment-specific topologies; sequences annotated to the United States were Iquitos virus rather than OROV. Two Italian sequences clustered with Cuban sequences across all three trees, concordant with published travel histories. Conclusions. Publicly available sequences contain phylogenetic structure that differs among the S, M, and L segment trees, but interpretation is constrained by uneven temporal, geographic, and host sampling and by the inclusion of reassortant species in a species-level dataset. The concentration of sequences from Brazil and human hosts, together with limited representation of non-human hosts, restricts inference about OROV diversity and ecology. Broader and more balanced genomic surveillance would improve the ability to resolve OROV evolutionary and transmission patterns.

papers.title: Mutation and Recombination Rates in Free-Ranging Polar Bears
papers.abstract: Mutation rate () and recombination rate (r) are fundamental population-genetic parameters, yet demographic and conservation inference in polar bears (Ursus maritimus) has relied on values borrowed from humans and other mammals. Known values vary by an order of magnitude across mammals, and inaccuracies in these estimates propagate into downstream analyses, such as inferences of demographic history. To address this, we used high-coverage whole-genome resequencing of eight parent-offspring trios from the Western Hudson Bay subpopulation of polar bears. We identified 329 de novo mutations and estimated a pedigree-based germline mutation rate of 1.22 x 10?? per site per generation, which is within the mammalian range and close to values previously assumed for this species. Trio-based phasing yielded 522 crossovers across 16 meioses (32.6 per meiosis), and a pedigree-inferred recombination rate of 1.50 cM/Mb. From 44 unrelated individuals sampled from the same subpopulation, we inferred a demography-aware recombination map with a length-weighted genome-wide recombination rate of 3.03 cM/Mb (median 1.28 cM/Mb). We also identified 8,515 recombination hotspot regions covering 2.10% of the genome, accounting for 43.8% of total map length, a 20.9-fold concentration. Crossovers overlapped LD-defined hotspots 5.06-fold more often than expected by chance (p < 0.001). Nucleotide diversity was low and positively rank-correlated with recombination rate, consistent with linked selection. Genomic features explained only ~3% of recombination rate variation, with GC content and SINE abundance the only significant predictors. These species-specific parameters provide an empirical foundation for future demographic reconstruction and population projection in this vulnerable, ice-obligate species.

papers.title: Chromosome-level genome assembly of Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica) reveals extensive centromeric satellite arrays
papers.abstract: We present a chromosome-level, haplotype-resolved genome assembly from Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica). The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes of 322 Mb and 295 Mb, with 89.7% and 95.6% respectively, each scaffolded into 7 chromosomes. Assembly completeness is high (BUSCO 97.8% in each haplotype), with 34,213 and 29,684 annotated protein-coding genes for haplotypes one and two, respectively. The chromosomes contain extensive centromeric satellite arrays that cover up to half of some chromosomes. Their precise functional boundaries remain undetermined.

papers.title: Pseudo-observations of longevity improve detection of resilience-associated genes in the Radiation Late Effects Cohort of rhesus macaques.
papers.abstract: Non-human primates are an ideal model for interrogating the genetic basis of human lifespan and resilience due to their long lifespan compared to other model organisms, development of similar age-related chronic conditions, and genetic similarity. However, like humans, statistical methods for modeling survival suffer from the challenges of dealing with non-proportionality of hazards, large numbers of living individuals that must be censored, and loss-to-follow-up over studies that may last a decade or more. Here we overcome these challenges through the use of pseudo-observations of Restricted Mean Survival Time as a measure of resilience to the acute challenge of radiation exposure and chronic challenges of aging and a Western-style diet in rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) from the Wake Forest Non-Human Primate Radiation Late Effects Cohort. Our whole-exome analysis used Genome-wide Efficient Mixed Model Association (GEMMA) to identify variants associated with longevity, and a subsequent Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) highlighted the cadherin and integrin signaling pathways as central to this resilience. As dysregulation of cell adhesion and extracellular matrix signaling is central to the development of fibrosis, we tested the functional relevance of these signals using a targeted Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD) score-weighted Sequence Kernel Association Test-Optimal (SKAT-O) analysis of GSEA leading-edge genes from both the cadherin and integrin pathways. This linked variant burden in PCDHGA5, PCDHGA3, PCDHGB2, PCDHA11, and PSENEN to the severity of myocardial fibrosis, and in IBSP, PDGFD, and LAMC2 to the severity of pulmonary fibrosis observed at necropsy. Critically, we note that the genetic variants are not caused by the radiation but rather create an underlying risk for disease that is then exacerbated by the acute and persistent stressors challenging these animals' intrinsic resilience. The success of this method in identifying biologically relevant genetic variants underlying survival in animals undergoing a strong challenge to their resilience highlights not only the role of genes predisposing animals to fibrosis in lifespan, but the overall utility of pseudo-observations in overcoming the limitations of survival analyses in humans and other long-lived species.

papers.title: Rapid environmental DNA detection with isothermal amplification methods: a comparison with the real-time quantitative PCR in the natterjack toad (Epidalea calamita).
papers.abstract: Species detection relying on environmental DNA (eDNA) traditionally relies on Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR). This amplification technique takes in general a minimum of one hour and requires in most cases access to specialized laboratories and equipment. Isothermal amplification techniques, originating from clinical research, are emerging as rapid and field-deployable alternative methods. Yet, whether their sensitivity, specificity, and cost/time-efficiency are comparable to the traditional real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) remains to be assessed. In this work, we compare the performance of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) and recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with qPCR to detect the natterjack toad (Epidalea calamita) from aquatic filtrations. This objective was achieved in three steps. First, we developed LAMP and RPA primers specific to the target species based on its mitochondrial genome. Second, we amplified DNA extracts from E. calamita and from tissues of closely related species using real-time fluorescence detection with LAMP, RPA, and qPCR commercially available protocols to evaluate and compare the sensitivity and specificity of the three methods. Finally, we validated all protocols on eDNA extracts recovered from water samples from ponds surveyed by field scientists. We show that RPA had a sensitivity equivalent to that of the qPCR, while LAMP sensitivity was ten times lower. All our assays amplified the species DNA in eDNA samples where the species was observed by field scientists. Through this work, we thus propose a robust methodology for implementing isothermal amplification assays for eDNA applications and show that RPA is a good alternative to qPCR for detecting conservation-priority species (i.e. protected or invasive species) when time and lab facilities are constrained.

papers.title: Genome assembly and characterization of two Brazilian soybean cultivars contrasting for stink bug resistance
papers.abstract: Brazil's tropical soybean germplasm still has few genomic resources: only one assembly of a Brazilian cultivar is available at NCBI. Here we describe chromosome-level de novo assemblies of two contrasting cultivars: IAC-100, described as resistant to phytophagous stink bugs, and CD-215, susceptible. We sequenced high molecular weight DNA using 10x Genomics linked reads, assembled the reads with Supernova, anchored the assembly to the Williams 82 reference with RaGOO and corrected structural errors with REAPR. The assemblies span 1.057 and 1.061 Gb, with scaffold N50 values of 53.6 and 54.2 Mb (48.0 and 47.7 Mb excluding gaps), and recover more than 97% of conserved plant genes assessed by BUSCO. Homology-based projection of the reference protein-coding genes generated 46,774 and 46,620 gene models. Comparing the proteomes of the two cultivars, we identified 2,002 divergent isoforms in 1,427 loci, classified by sequence divergence, length variation, combined divergence and non-conserved homology. These data expand the genomic resources for tropical soybean germplasm, still underrepresented in public databases, and for studies of insect resistance.

papers.title: A genomic prediction framework for growth traits in black soldier fly (Hermetia illucens) breeding programmes
papers.abstract: Background Genomic prediction has been applied in livestock, plant and aquaculture species to accelerate genetic gain. However, its application and potential still remain unexplored in farmed black soldier fly (BSF), an emerging globally important insect production species. Due to the diversity of BSF feed sources, selection strategies need to be evaluated across various feedstocks and production environments to aid in building genomic selection into BSF breeding programmes. In this study, 2,083 BSF larvae from the base population were reared on three diets (SYK: Soy-okara, BSG: brewers' spent grain and FVW: fruit and vegetable waste), and 536 from the F7 population were reared on a chicken starter feed diet. Larvae were phenotyped for four growth traits (LBW, larval body weight; LL, larval length; LW, larval width; LSA, larval surface area) and genotyped across 4,680 SNPs. Genomic prediction was evaluated using seven methods under additive (A) and additive-dominance (AD) models, considering across- and within-diet effects, genotype by diet (G x D) interactions, differences amongst reference and test generations, and SNP densities. Results Performance varied across all scenarios, with LBW showing higher predictive ability (PA) among the growth traits. Accounting for dominance generally improved PA. Multivariate models accounting for G x D performed similarly to, or marginally better than, within-diet predictions. Cross-diet prediction was more variable and generally lower than within-diet prediction, showing reduced transferability across untested nutritional environments. Reducing the SNP density from 4,680 to 3,000 SNPs maintained comparable PA; however, PA decreased below 3,000 SNPs. Across multiple generations, predictive performance declined, resulting from reduced genetic connectivity and possible genotype-by-environment (G x E) interactions between the reference and testing populations. Conclusions Overall, these results provide an application-based framework for genomic prediction in BSF in semi- or commercial production settings. Results also highlight the importance of the genetic model, representative reference populations, and appropriate marker densities for genomic selection.

papers.title: The tiger shark, Galeocerdo cuvier (Peron & Lesueur, 1822), genome reveals genomic and epigenomic signatures of shark evolution and demographic history
papers.abstract: Cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes) represent one of the oldest extant vertebrate lineages, persisting for over 450 million years, yet genomic resources remain limited for many species despite widespread conservation concern. The tiger shark, Galeocerdo cuvier (Peron & Lesueur, 1822), the sole surviving member of the family Galeocerdonidae, is a circumglobally cosmopolitan predator vital in ecosystem regulation but is experiencing population declines. Here, we generated the first chromosome-scale haplotype-phased reference genome for the tiger shark and integrated comparative and population genomics with methylomics to characterise its genome architecture and evolutionary history. This assembly presented the first evidence of male heterogamety in this species. Comparative analyses revealed lineage-specific transposable element expansions across the chondrichthyan class suggesting ongoing genome restructuring in Carcharhiniform sharks. We report the first hydroxymethylome in a chondrichthyan, higher than that of other vertebrates, hinting at novel DNA evolutionary and regulatory pathways in an early-diverging lineage of jawed vertebrates. We identified genomic signatures of prolonged population decline that correlated with historical climate fluctuations and have resulted in sustained low levels of genetic heterozygosity in this species. These findings offer new insights into shark and broader vertebrate genomic and epigenomic evolution while providing valuable resources for conservation genomics of one of the world's most widespread top-order predators in the face of accelerating environmental change.

papers.title: SPACE-Tag Enables High-Throughput Spatial Chromatin Profiling With CUT&Tag
papers.abstract: Spatial epigenomics maps chromatin states within intact tissues, yet current methods remain limited by accessibility and scale. We developed SPACE-Tag, a spatial CUT&Tag framework that converts epigenetic marks-associated DNA into polyadenylated RNA through T7 based linear amplification, enabling direct integration with standard spatial transcriptomic workflows. Applied to the mouse brain, SPACETag resolved activating and repressive chromatin landscapes, recovered region-specific gene regulatory programs across anatomical domains, and showed strong correlation with existing bulk and single cell reference data. We generated an integrated multimodal atlas of the aging mouse brain, profiling five histone modifications and the transcriptome in parallel across the adult lifespan to establish the largest spatial multimodal dataset to date. This analysis uncovered sharp regional divergence with aging in the brain: fiber tracts showed widespread transcriptional downregulation, often without nearby chromatin state transitions, whereas the isocortex showed coordinated chromatin transcriptome changes, including an H3K4me1 peak module that increased with age, was enriched at super-enhancers and linked to upregulation of neuronal plasticity regulators. These findings highlight the power of multimodal and high throughput spatial genomics in uncovering the divergent regulatory logic that governs tissue-specific vulnerability and resilience in the aging brain.

papers.title: Genome-wide Analysis of the VQ Gene Family and Expression Profiling in Sorghum bicolor
papers.abstract: Soil salinization severely restricts agricultural productivity, making the stress-tolerant sorghum an ideal model for studying crop adaptation. VQ motif-containing proteins are plant-specific transcriptional co-regulators vital for stress responses, yet their roles in sorghum remain underexplored. Here, we identified 35 VQ genes in sorghum, classifying them into seven subfamilies. Evolutionary analysis indicated that the family's expansion was primarily driven by segmental duplication. Notably, synteny analysis revealed a lack of collinearity between sorghum and Arabidopsis VQ genes, suggesting significant functional divergence during monocot evolution. Expression profiling showed distinct patterns among VQ members, with SbVQ34, SbVQ39 adn SbVQ40 significantly upregulated under salt stress. Furthermore, protein-protein interaction analysis highlighted SbVQ39 as a potential key regulator in sorghum salt tolerance. This study provides novel insights into sorghum's salinity tolerance mechanisms and establishes a foundation for utilizing VQ genes in breeding salt-tolerant crops.

papers.title: Measuring American black bear genetic load in fixed structural variants and runs of homozygosity
papers.abstract: Populations living in geographically isolated regions are expected to have reduced gene flow, increased genetic drift, and elevated levels of inbreeding, influencing both genetic load and possibly the distribution of structural variants. The American black bear (Ursus americanus) is widely found across Ontario, Canada, where populations inhabit diverse landscapes ranging from relatively intact contiguous forested landscapes to isolated regions such as the Saugeen Peninsula. Here, we investigated the population genomic history across five Ontario black bear populations using a combination of short-read (SR) and long-read (LR) sequencing data. We compared population genetic metrics including nucleotide diversity ({pi}), Tajimas D, runs of homozygosity (ROH), and genome-wide structural variants (SVs) to assess population health and identify signatures of isolation. Our results showed that the isolated Saugeen Peninsula population is genetically distinct and exhibited reduced nucleotide diversity, greater ROH and SV abundance compared with mainland populations. The population also showed elevated genetic load in all genomic features, suggesting increased exposure of deleterious variation that are expressed in ROH and population specific SVs. We further discuss the integration of ROH, SVs and genetic load in conservation assessments.

papers.title: How mutation rate evolves: Gene expression shapes genome-wide mutation rates in Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans
papers.abstract: Mutation rates vary across the genome, linked to biochemical properties of local DNA sequences. However, mutation rate variation also associates with functional genomic features, raising the possibility that intragenomic mutation rate variation is shaped by adaptive evolution. In particular, recent studies in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana suggested that highly conserved genes under strong purifying selection also have reduced de novo mutation rates, suggesting that natural selection may have acted to reduce mutation rate specifically at important genes. However, whether this is true for wider taxa, including animals, remains unknown. Here we repurposed published mutation accumulation datasets from Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans to investigate the determinants of de novo single nucleotide variant (DNV) rates genome-wide under minimal selection. Loci under stronger purifying selection accumulated fewer mutations, including intronic and synonymous mutations. Various sequence-specific (i.e. GC content) and regulatory features (e.g. chromatin modifications) were strongly correlated with mutation rate, but gene expression best explained the depletion of mutations within strongly conserved loci, even after accounting for correlations amongst variables. Using excision repair (XR)-sequencing data we determined that higher levels of transcription- coupled repair (TCR) were associated with reduced mutation rates, strongly suggesting that TCR lowers mutation rate of highly conserved genes. Furthermore, by comparing orthologs between C. elegans and its close relative Pristionchus pacificus, we found that altered gene expression across evolutionary time correlated with altered mutation rate. These findings support a model whereby developmental transcription modulates local mutation rates through TCR. A corollary is that adaptive mutation bias may emerge indirectly, downstream of gene regulation evolution, providing a mechanistic framework that reconciles non-random local mutation rate variation with established evolutionary theory.

papers.title: Isoform diversity as a complementary dimension of gene expression
papers.abstract: Most human genes produce multiple mRNA isoforms through alternative splicing and alternative transcription start and end sites. Isoforms of the same gene can differ in function, and their relative abundance varies between tissues and conditions. However, gene expression analysis is often restricted to the gene level, masking its diversification into mRNA and protein isoforms with potentially distinct functionality. Here we show, using an adaptation of Shannon evenness applied to 4,814 GTEx samples from 25 tissues, that isoform diversity constitutes a distinct dimension of gene expression, complementary to gene-level abundance and whole transcriptome diversity. Isoform diversity separated tissues based on non-differentially expressed genes and changed with age in a gene- and tissue-specific manner, most strongly in the brain and often without changes in overall gene expression levels. During neuronal differentiation, it increased most notably in RNA processing and splicing genes. Our results suggest that isoform diversity represents an independent dimension of gene expression and may help explain functional differences between tissues and cell states that are not captured by analyzing expression levels alone.

papers.title: Somatic structural variation discovery on cancer pangenome graphs
papers.abstract: Somatic structural variants (SVs) drive tumorigenesis across most cancers, yet low variant allele frequencies in subclonal populations often necessitate multi-sample sequencing per patient. Existing somatic SV callers rely on whole-genome read alignments against a single linear reference, incurring high computational costs and reference bias. We present JANUS, which discovers somatic SVs directly within a personal pangenome, a colored de Bruijn-like graph of locally consistent parsing (LCP) cores built from matched normal and tumor PacBio HiFi reads. JANUS identifies candidate SV sites traversed exclusively by tumor reads without prior alignment, mapping only short read snippets surrounding each site. Across five tumor-normal pairs in the CASTLE panel, JANUS leads the 18-caller consensus with a mean F1 score of 0.887 (next-best caller: 0.858), widening its lead under low-signal regimes (0.489 versus 0.362 at 5x; 0.683 versus 0.520 at 20% purity). End to end, JANUS analyzes a tumor-normal pair in ~11 minutes on average with 16 threads, which is ~24x faster than read alignment alone on the same machine. In a 20-tumor patient simulation, joint graph calling outperforms independent pairwise runs in speed and accuracy, particularly at low depth. By processing multi-sample cohorts jointly and maintaining sensitivity at low coverage and purity, JANUS provides an efficient, reference-unbiased framework for cancer genomics. JANUS is available at https://github.com/BilkentCompGen/janus.

papers.title: Multi-omics integration reveals candidate genes and molecular mechanisms associated with resistance to sugarcane smut
papers.abstract: Sugarcane smut, caused by the fungus Sporisorium scitamineum (Syd.), is one of the main diseases affecting sugarcane and is capable of causing severe yield losses in susceptible varieties. Given the limitations of classical breeding, mainly due to the genetic complexity of sugarcane cultivars, molecular and omics approaches have gained increasing prominence for studying the genetic basis of traits such as disease resistance. In this context, we investigated sugarcane resistance to smut through the integration of association mapping methods and transcriptomics. A panel of 155 genotypes was genotyped with 33,335 SNP markers and inoculated with S. scitamineum generating three phenotypic variables. These data were jointly analyzed through genome-wide association analyses to identify marker-trait associations. In addition, transcriptomic analyses were performed using publicly available datasets from four studies evaluating sugarcane responses to smut. The integration of these multi-omics data enabled the identification of candidate genes involved in structural reinforcement, immune signaling, redox homeostasis, genome maintenance, and cellular adaptation. These findings provide valuable molecular resources for functional validation and breeding strategies aimed at developing sugarcane cultivars with enhanced smut resistance.

papers.title: Disparities in avian genomic resources highlight gaps across the Global South
papers.abstract: Avian genomes have proliferated rapidly in recent years while expanding our knowledge of genomic evolution. However, evaluating bird sampling across the tree of life and across their distributions is necessary to assess their contributions to global bird diversity and diversification patterns. We evaluated all available avian genome assemblies across geography, taxonomy, conservation status, and time. The 1,712 species with at least one genome assembly represent only ~15% of recognized avian diversity. Although all orders were represented, 24 bird families (all restricted to the Global South) lacked any genome assembly, and only ~37% (N= 2,397) of recognized genera had genomic representation. Nearly 78% of the most evolutionarily distinct and globally endangered (EDGE) lineages lacked a genome. Genomic resources are concentrated in temperate regions of the Global North, whereas species-rich tropical regions in Africa, South America, and Southeast Asia remain severely underrepresented relative to their diversity. Even after accounting for conservation status, evolutionary distinctiveness, and ecology, Global South species had roughly fourfold lower odds of having a genome than Global North species. Notably, the post-2021 surge in genome sequencing has counter-intuitively widened this gap. Together, our results highlight persistent gaps in genomic resources across the Global South and the need to collectively address these global knowledge gaps via collaborative efforts.

papers.title: Plumage diversity without differential expression of pigmentation genes in a rapid avian radiation
papers.abstract: Uncovering the molecular basis of reproductive traits is key to understanding species divergence. Capuchino Seedeaters ( Sporophila ), a radiation of genetically similar birds differing mainly in male reproductive plumage color, can be leveraged to study how such traits evolve. Outlier scans identified candidate pigmentation variants primarily in noncoding sequence, implying regulatory changes. However, RNA-seq of growing feather follicles generally did not show differential expression of pigmentation genes among different colors, with only ASIP downregulated in crown feathers. Gene expression patterns instead varied by body region. The largest difference between dimorphic sexes was the upregulation of the carotenoid-degrading gene BCO2 in males, accompanied by lower carotenoid content in male feathers. An improved genome annotation assigned 9.5% of candidate variants into coding and untranslated sequence. This suggests species-diagnostic variants lie within transcribed sequence and could act post-transcriptionally, rather than through transcript abundance, leading to a revised hypothesis for plumage divergence in this radiation.

papers.title: A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of paper wasp brains highlights Kenyon cells' role in social behavior
papers.abstract: Social insects provide unique opportunities for studying social interactions, but the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying these behaviors are poorly understood. Here, we performed single-cell sequencing to profile the transcriptomes of 96,310 cells across four phenotypes of Polistes fuscatus paper wasps: foundresses, workers, gynes, and males, to determine how social states and social interactions are encoded in the physiology of the central brain. We characterized the cellular diversity of the Polistes brain and demonstrate that a substantial portion of the brain is composed of diverse populations of Kenyon cell neurons. The composition and gene-expression profiles of these Kenyon cells, as well other neural and non-neural cell populations, vary across sex, caste, and season. We also demonstrate that social interactions, and even the mere observation of a social interaction, induce significant transcriptomic responses, including signatures of neural activation, across populations of Kenyon cell neurons. Notably, the transcriptional and activational signatures elicited by observing a social interaction frequently overlapped with those induced by direct social interaction, suggesting that a shared neural program underlies both direct social interactions and social observation.

papers.title: Structural Variant Aware Identity-by-Descent Detection on Pangenome Graphs
papers.abstract: Identity-by-descent (IBD) detection identifies genomic segments inherited from a common ancestor, and supports studies of relatedness, demographic history, and disease mapping. Existing methods primarily use linear genome representations and do not identify structural variants (SVs) shared within IBD segments. Pangenome graphs encode SVs and store each haplotype as a path through the graph. We present GIBD (Graph Identity-by-Descent), which detects IBD segments in the Graph Burrows-Wheeler Transform (GBWT) of a pangenome graph and annotates each detected segment with the SVs it carries. GIBD enumerates the pairwise-maximal exact matches between all pairs of haplotype paths in a single traversal of the GBWT, and visits each shared subpath once. On graphs of bounded degree, the traversal takes time linear in the number of nodes on the haplotype paths and the number of matches it enumerates. On a standard IBD benchmark, the power and accuracy of GIBD are within 0.009 and 0.001 of hap-ibd, a widely used linear method. Compared with impop_k, a pangenome-based IBD method, GIBD detects more 2-4 cM segments and runs in 33 seconds instead of 9.6 hours. In simulations of 1,000 haplotypes built from assemblies of the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC), the insertion, deletion, and inversion labels of GIBD have a precision of 1.000, with and without assembly error. In a real four-generation family, GIBD identifies the inherited allele on parent-offspring segments at all 3,235 SVs on chromosome 20 where the parent is heterozygous, and reports no IBD between unrelated members. It also tracks a disease-associated 900-kb inversion at 17q21.31 across three generations and correctly labels all segments that share it. GIBD makes SVs visible in IBD detection from pangenome graphs.

papers.title: Contrasting Range and Demographic Histories in two Palearctic Dragonfly Species (Odonata: Anisoptera)
papers.abstract: Climatic suitability is often used to infer historical range changes, yet whether suitable area predicts effective population size remains unexplored. We investigated this relationship in two Palearctic dragonflies with contrasting ecologies: Somatochlora arctica, a widespread peatland specialist, and S. meridionalis, a southern European species associated with shaded streams. We combined demographic reconstructions from individual reference genomes using the pairwise sequentially Markovian coalescent (PSMC), maximum entropy (MaxEnt) species distribution models projected across six paleoclimatic intervals spanning approximately 3.3 million years, and ancestral state reconstructions of peatland specialization. Predicted suitable area was consistently greater for S. arctica, reaching its greatest extent during the Last Glacial Maximum. However, its inferred effective population size was smaller than that of S. meridionalis for most of the last ~275,000 years. Ancestral reconstructions placed the most probable gain of peatland specialization in the S. arctica lineage (Clade I) during the late Miocene, with a median age of 9.4 million years, predating the modeled climatic intervals. These findings indicate a decoupling of climatic suitability and demographic history. Patchy breeding habitat, population structure, and the isolated Scottish origin of the sampled S. arctica may contribute to this mismatch. Combining genomic, ecological, and phylogenetic approaches provides complementary insights into historical biogeography and highlights the limitations of interpreting suitable climate as available breeding habitat or using individual genomes to characterize species-wide demographic histories.

papers.title: Transcriptome reallocation during infection reshapes synonymous codon demand in Botrytis cinerea
papers.abstract: While genomic codon usage is fixed within an individual isolate, the synonymous codons represented in its RNA pool can change when transcription shifts among genes. We tested whether this transcript-level phenotype accompanies infection by reanalyzing 39 libraries from three public Botrytis cinerea RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) time series in S. lycopersicum, Arabidopsis thaliana, and Physcomitrium patens. Gene counts were corrected for coding length, combined with fixed gene-specific codon inventories, and analyzed as centered log ratios within synonymous amino-acid families. Sampling time accounted for 95-98% of fungal codon-demand variation in each series. The association persisted after effective-length correction, unique-only competitive mapping, host-homology exclusion, depth equalization, protein-family weighting, and removal of translation-associated genes. Change vectors over the interpolated, time-aligned 16-24-h interval were positively aligned among studies, whereas later trajectories diverged. Matched reassignments of complete expression trajectories showed more full-series organization than expected in S. lycopersicum and Arabidopsis, but not in P. patens. Codon-preference-weighted abundance and expression breadth also changed through infection, although their directions were not universal. Across systems, large non-translation contributors repeatedly carried ATP-synthase/respiratory and extracellular annotations, although their timing and companion functions differed. Infection-associated transcriptional reallocation therefore repeatedly restructures the synonymous composition of the inferred fungal transcript pool. This establishes a dynamic allocation phenotype and a basis for testing consequences for RNA stability and translation during host-pathogen interactions.

papers.title: Genomic characterization and evolutionary path of human satellite 1B in primates highlight a dynamic relationship with transposable elements
papers.abstract: Human Satellite 1B (HSat1B) remains one of the least characterized classical human satellite DNAs, despite its massive abundance on the human Y chromosome. Its tripartite ~2.5 kb monomer - comprising an AluY fragment, a GC-rich unit (here named H1B) and an AT-rich block - points to an evolutionary origin tightly linked to transposable elements (TEs). Here, we present the first comprehensive comparative genomic, phylogenetic and transcriptional characterization of HSat1B across 10 primate species using Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) and chromosome-scale long-read assemblies, combined with DNA-FISH, RNA-FISH and long-read transcriptomic analyses. We demonstrate that while canonical tandem HSat1B arrays are restricted to Homininae (human, chimpanzee, bonobo and gorilla), the core H1B unit and its structural variants (H1Bsv1 and H1Bsv2) occur across all 10 primate genomes, including strepsirrhines (lemur). This indicates that the H1B sequence predates the assembly of the composite HSat1B monomer by at least 60 million years. H1B variants consistently map within TE-rich genomic contexts, supporting a stepwise, TE-mediated model of satellite diversification and mobilization. Within Homininae, humans exhibit a dramatic lineage-specific expansion driven by Yq12 amplification (~14.2 Mb; 92% of total genomic content), whereas non-human great apes carry smaller, highly polymorphic autosomal and Y-linked arrays. Finally, we show that H1B-containing sequences are transcriptionally active in human and gorilla nuclei via RNA-FISH and characterize heterogeneous H1B/Alu chimeric non-coding transcripts in the human male germline. Collectively, our findings uncover the birth and Homininae-specific expansion of a composite satellite DNA seeded by an ancient primate sequence module and sculpted by transposable elements.
